title: Backdrop Between Poles
story: A photographer works in a park with a row of wooden poles of different heights, exactly 1 metre apart. She wants to stretch one rectangular backdrop between two of them.

The backdrop is as wide as the gap between the poles and only as tall as the shorter one, or it sags. Poles in between do not matter; it hangs in front of them. Which two poles give the biggest backdrop?
task: Write widestBackdrop(heights). heights[i] is the height of pole i. For two poles i < j, the backdrop area is (j - i) × min(heights[i], heights[j]). Return the largest possible area.
If there are fewer than two poles, return 0.

examples.explanation: Poles 1 (height 7) and 5 (height 8) are 4 metres apart, and the shorter is 7: 4 × 7 = 28. The two ends give only 6 × 1 = 6, because pole 6 is so short.
The tall neighbours 10 and 9 give 1 × 9 = 9. Wider pairs are held down by a short pole: 2 and 9 give 2 × 2 = 4, 2 and 1 give 3 × 1 = 3.

hints: Start with the widest pair, the end poles of [3, 7, 2, 6, 4, 8, 1]: area 6 × 1 = 6. The short right pole limits it. Could any other pair using that pole do better?
Any other pair with the height-1 pole is narrower and still at most 1 tall. That pole can never beat 6, so throw it away.
This holds in general: of the two end poles, the shorter one has had its best chance.
Put left at the first pole and right at the last. Record the area, then move the pointer on the shorter pole one step inward. Repeat until they meet, keeping the largest area.
bruteForce: Try every pair of poles and keep the largest area.
With 10,000 poles that is about 50 million pairs. Most are hopeless: a pair whose short pole was already paired with something farther away can never win, yet brute force checks it anyway.

walkthrough: Start with the widest backdrop, the two end poles. Any other partner for the shorter one is closer, with the height still capped by that pole, so it can never beat this area. Drop it and move inward.
• Poles 0 and 6 (3 and 1): 6 × 1 = 6. Best = 6. Pole 6 is shorter, so move right to 5.
• Poles 0 and 5 (3 and 8): 5 × 3 = 15. Best = 15. Pole 0 is shorter, so move left to 1.
• Poles 4 and 5 (4 and 8): 1 × 4 = 4. Move left to 5. The pointers meet. Answer: 28.
Six pairs measured instead of all 21. The classic mistake is moving the taller pole: that throws away a pole that might still be in the best pair.
solution.timeWhy: Each step moves one pointer inward, so there are n - 1 steps.
solution.spaceWhy: Two pointers and the best area.
solution.takeaway: Start two pointers at the ends and at each step discard the side that provably cannot be in a better answer. The proof is the whole trick: once one end has had its best chance, drop it.
